His Work, Halakhic Teaching and Kabbalistic Doctrine of Rabbi Yehuda Fetaya: A Historical, Philosophical and Practical Analysis

This source surveys the life and extensive teachings of Rabbi Yehuda Fetaya, one of the great kabbalists in Baghdad and Jerusalem, focusing on the uniqueness of practical kabbalah and his metaphysical thought. The text presents his philosophical structure around the rectification of souls, reincarnations and the struggle against forces of impurity, alongside detailed documentation of exorcism rituals and dream interpretations he performed throughout his years of leadership. Additionally, the survey emphasizes the Rabbi's public and spiritual involvement during the Holocaust through prayers and liturgical poems, and provides a bibliographical analysis of his central compositions which constitute an invaluable asset in kabbalistic literature. Finally, the source describes the chain of generations he left behind, which continues to this day to influence the religious, cultural and academic sphere in Israel.

His Work, Halakhic Teaching and Kabbalistic Doctrine of Rabbi Yehuda Fetaya: A Historical, Philosophical and Practical Analysis

Biography and Early Path of Rabbi Yehuda Fetaya in Baghdad

Rabbi Yehuda Moshe Yeshua Fetaya was born in Baghdad in the Ottoman Empire on the 2nd of Shevat 5619 (January 7, 1859), as the third son of the kabbalist Rabbi Moshe Yeshua and his wife Hannah.[1, 2, 3] From his earliest childhood, exceptional talents and a deep aspiration for a life of asceticism and religious devotion were evident in him.[1] He received his primary education at the local "Midrash Talmud Torah," and upon maturity moved to study at the "Midrash Beit Zilkha" yeshiva, which was the central Torah center of Babylonian Jewry at that time.[1, 3, 4] During this period he absorbed the teachings of the community's spiritual leader, Rabbi Yosef Hayyim of Baghdad (the "Ben Ish Hai"), whose sermons he regularly attended and who later became his principal master in esoteric teachings.[3, 4]

A formative event in Rabbi Yehuda Fetaya's life occurred when he was only seventeen years old.[1, 4] He was asked to serve as cantor in the beit midrash of the rosh yeshiva, Rabbi Abdallah Somekh.[1] One of those present in the congregation expressed opposition to the appointment on the grounds that this was a young man whose beard had not yet grown fully.[1] In response to this protest, Rabbi Abdallah Somekh rose and ordained him on the spot as rabbi and halakhic decisor, thereby giving public validation to his precocious Torah greatness.[1] This ordination paved the way for Rabbi Yehuda as one of the leading great Torah scholars in Baghdad, and these biographical details were later documented in the composition of Sh. N. Gottlieb, "Oholei Shem" ("Tents of the Name"), printed in Pinsk in 1912.[5]

While engaged in revealed Torah and halakhic decision-making, Rabbi Yehuda Fetaya began to delve secretly into the study of kabbalah.[1] By age twenty-five he already possessed outstanding expertise in both revealed and concealed teachings, and published his first composition in kabbalah, "Yein HaRekah" ("Wine of Ointment").[1] His thought was deeply influenced by Lurianic kabbalah, which he later interpreted in his monumental composition "Beit Lehem Yehuda" ("House of Bread of Judah").[4, 6] Alongside his theoretical study, Rabbi Yehuda Fetaya developed a unique practical approach to kabbalah, which included writing amulets, healing the sick through incantations and prayers, dream interpretation, and performing "soul rectifications" for the deceased.[1, 4]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Metaphysics of the World of Souls: Reincarnation, Rectification and Forces of Impurity

The kabbalistic doctrine of Rabbi Yehuda Fetaya is based on a dynamic and intensive conception of the world of souls and their passage between worlds.[7, 8] According to his system, the human soul does not complete its function with the death of the physical body, but rather is subject to a complex system of judgments and refinements.[8, 9] Souls that sinned or did not complete their destiny in this world are required to undergo processes of purging transgressions, foremost among them the punishment of "kaf ha-kela" ("the hollow of the sling"), Gehinnom, or return to the world through reincarnation.[10, 11]

Rabbi Yehuda Fetaya elaborated on the question of reincarnations and the need to complete the 248 positive commandments.[10] He clarified that a person who did not fulfill positive commandments that were within his ability to perform (such as tsitsit and tefillin), is compelled to return in reincarnation time after time until he fulfills them completely.[10] In contrast, for commandments that cannot be fulfilled in the present time, such as Temple service, the soul does not return in reincarnation.[10]

A fascinating aspect of his doctrine deals with the reincarnation of souls in foods.[10] According to his teaching, certain souls may be reincarnated in plants or animals, and if a person eats such food with proper kabbalistic intention, he is able to rectify the reincarnated soul and release it from its distress.[10] Conversely, eating without proper intention can cause severe spiritual harm, whereby the reincarnated soul negatively influences the person and arouses in him impulses to sin as it sinned in its lifetime.[10]

Personal testimony illustrating his deep belief in reincarnation and spiritual diagnosis relates to Rabbi Yehuda's son.[10] The kabbalist Rabbi Avraham Ades revealed to Rabbi Yehuda Fetaya that his son was the reincarnation of a rabbi who had beaten his students in this world.[10] When the son fell ill, Rabbi Yehuda approached him and told him that he must make confession and complete his spiritual rectification in light of this revelation.[10] The son indeed accepted these words, confessed, and passed from the world with acceptance and rectification.[10]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Struggle Against Dibbukim: Exorcism of Spirits and Metaphysical Dialogues

One of the most famous aspects of Rabbi Yehuda Fetaya's work is his direct confrontation with the phenomenon of the "dibbuk"—the penetration of a sinful and suffering soul into the body of a living person.[1, 4, 8] Rabbi Yehuda developed a systematic practice based on kabbalistic "unifications" (yiḥudim), blowing of shofars and recitation of prayers in the presence of a large congregation.[8] The purpose of the exorcism ritual was not only to save the one possessed by the dibbuk, but also to grant rectification and mercy to the reincarnated soul itself in order to enable it to enter Gehinnom or Gan Eden and cease its wandering in kaf ha-kela.[8, 11] In modern research literature this work has received comprehensive analysis, such as the article by Professor Yehuda Liebes and articles in academic journals dealing with the magical and exorcistic aspects of his kabbalah.[3]

Below is a detailed account of major cases in which Rabbi Yehuda Fetaya intervened, presenting the different methods of confrontation and the metaphysical complexity of the rituals:

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Orders of Rectifications and Dream Interpretation

Rabbi Yehuda Fetaya established a complete teaching directed toward saving the souls of the deceased, particularly those who did not observe Torah and commandments in their lifetimes and are in great distress in the world of truth.[7, 9] He distinguished between different types of rectifications and defined the spiritual conditions for their performance:

The Great Rectification of the Deceased: A complex and structured prayer order intended for ten adult men.[7, 11] The rectification includes recitation of the entire Book of Psalms with internal division into circuits, recitation of a special text for rectification of the deceased that the Rabbi composed, and addition of "annulment of vows and curses" for the deceased.[7, 11, 12] Its purpose is to save the soul from ḥibbut ha-kever (torment of the grave), from kaf ha-kela, from difficult reincarnations and from Gehinnom.[11] The rectification is usually performed on erev Rosh Ḥodesh (minor Yom Kippur) or during the Ten Days of Repentance.[7, 13]

The Short Rectification of the Deceased: An abridged prayer order that Rabbi Yehuda composed for one who cannot organize a minyan of ten men.[11, 14] The uniqueness of this rectification is that even an individual can recite it in his home, and it includes a focused request that the deceased no longer be in a state of "naked and bare" in the world of souls.[14]

In his books it is emphasized that the ability to identify the precise defect in the soul of the deceased and to rectify it directly was unique to righteous individuals at the level of Rabbi Yehuda Fetaya.[9] For this reason, the study and prayers performed today by various organizations under the name "rectification of the deceased" constitute primarily acts of charity, study of Mishnayot, public recitation of Psalms and recitation of memorial prayer for the merit of the deceased, which greatly benefit the soul but are not completely identical to the original and personal practice
that the rabbi himself performed.[9]

Alongside rectifications for the deceased, Rabbi Yehudah Fetaya functioned as a distinguished dream interpreter.[1, 4] He devoted a substantial portion of his writings to the metaphysical distinction between dreams originating in the human soul or in forces of impurity and demons, and prophetic dreams or those sent from heaven to hint to a person about his sins or about the need of a deceased relative for rectification.[5] Many flocked to his doorstep in order to merit the interpretation of their dreams and the performance of "dream rectification" to remove harsh decrees.[1, 4]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Immigration to Jerusalem and Spiritual Mobilization During the Shoah

Rabbi Yehudah Fetaya aspired to immigrate to the Land of Israel throughout his entire life.[1] He immigrated twice to Jerusalem but was compelled to return to Baghdad due to the Jerusalem climate, which did not suit his fragile state of health.[1] In the year 5694 (1933) he immigrated a third time and settled in Jerusalem permanently, where he operated and led the fellowship of kabbalists until his final day.[1, 3, 4]

With the outbreak of the Second World War and the arrival of shocking reports about the annihilation of European Jewry, alongside the advance of the Nazi army under Rommel's command in North Africa toward the gates of the Land of Israel, Rabbi Yehudah Fetaya enlisted in intensive spiritual activity for the rescue of the Jewish yishuv.[3, 15] He viewed these events as an immediate existential threat and organized mass prayers and orders of "Tikkun Ḥatzot" (Midnight Rectification) at Rachel's Tomb in Efrat.[3] For him, Rachel's Tomb represented the national focal point of mercy, the place where the mother weeping over her children could arouse heavenly mercy and prevent bloodshed.[3, 16]

In the year 5700 (1940), in light of the decrees, he printed the booklet "Maḥberet Asire ha-Tikva" (Notebook of the Prisoners of Hope) (and in 1942 "Maḥberet Asire ha-Tefillot" [Notebook of the Prisoners of Prayers]).[3, 15] In these booklets he collected orders of petitions for mercy and prayers for times of trouble, with a call for spiritual unity of the entire public for the rescue of the nation.[15]

From this spiritual activity emerged his famous liturgical poem "Zekhut Raḥel" (The Merit of Rachel).[3, 16] This poem possesses extraordinary dramatic power, depicting Rachel our matriarch emerging from her grave and wandering among the patriarchs of the nation, Moses our Teacher, Joshua son of Nun, and the kings of the House of David, in order to demand from them answers about the fate of her children being led to slaughter.[16] Only when she turns directly to the Holy One, Blessed be He, and refuses to be comforted, is a voice heard from heaven promising her that there is reward for her action and her children will return to their border.[16] The poem became an iron-clad asset in the liturgy of the Mizrahi communities in times of trouble and on selihot days.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Bibliographic Analysis of His Writings and Kabbalistic Compositions

The compositions of Rabbi Yehudah Fetaya are considered masterpieces of Lurianic kabbalistic literature, combining philological precision in the writings of the Ari and the Rashash together with phenomenology of the practical world.[6, 8, 17]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Generational Dynasty and Spiritual and Cultural Continuity

Rabbi Yehudah Fetaya and his wife Jahala Rachel left behind them an extensive family that continued his kabbalistic and public path.[3] Among his children, his son Ḥakham Shaul Fetaya stood out, who functioned as a kabbalist, writer of amulets, and dream interpreter.[3, 18, 19] Ḥakham Shaul conducted his activity from his shop and from the synagogue "Minḥat Yehudah" in Jerusalem, and even personally performed several dybbuk exorcisms in his father's manner.[19] He was known as a folk healer who diagnosed illnesses according to a person's wrist pulse, classifying the source of the illness into three central categories: panic, distress, or physical illness.[19]

The legacy of Rabbi Yehudah Fetaya continues to influence the religious, scholarly, and cultural sphere in Israel through his many descendants and great-grandchildren, whose details were documented in memorial books such as "Arze ha-Levanon" (Jerusalem, 5766) [3]:

Rabbi David Batzri: The rabbi's great-grandson, who serves as head of the kabbalists' yeshiva "ha-Shalom" in Jerusalem and is considered one of the most senior kabbalists of our generation, continuing in practice the tradition of performing rectifications for the deceased and dybbuk exorcism.[3]

Rabbi Ezra Batzri: The rabbi's great-grandson, served as a member of the Supreme Rabbinical Court and chief rabbi of the rabbinical court in Jerusalem, and author of many halakhic works.[3]

Rabbi Yitzḥak Batzri: The rabbi's great-grandson, author of dozens of books on halakha, aggadah, and kabbalah.[3]

Professor Ḥaviva Pedaya: The rabbi's great-granddaughter, a world-renowned kabbalah scholar, professor at Ben-Gurion University, poet and author who integrates the legacy of Mizrahi kabbalah in her research.[3]

Ḥana Fetaya: The rabbi's great-granddaughter, music and liturgical poetry scholar who promotes the preservation of the kabbalistic song and melody traditions of Babylonian Jews.[3]

Asaf Pedaya: The rabbi's great-grandson, contractor and entrepreneur involved in construction and development in the Land.[3]

Rabbi Yehudah Ovadiah: The rabbi's great-grandson, served as rabbi of the "Orot ha-Ḥoma" community in the Har Ḥoma neighborhood of Jerusalem and as rabbi at the Western Wall yeshiva, and died of cancer on the 4th of Ḥeshvan 5775.[3]

Moshe Barazani: The grandson of Rabbi Yehudah Fetaya, one of those who ascended the gallows and member of the Etzel underground, who set himself on fire in the cell of Jerusalem prison together with Meir Feinstein in order to prevent their hanging by the British.[3]

The figure of Rabbi Yehudah Fetaya remains in the eyes of halakhic authorities and kabbalists as a symbol of a rare combination of meticulous scholarship, systematic writing, and absolute devotion to rescuing sinful and suffering souls, an activity that continues to resonate in the works and deeds of his descendants.[3, 4, 7]
